html:
A Sri Lankan Buddhist reformer and writer, born in Colombo in 1864 and died at Sarnath in India in 1933. He led the modern revival of Buddhism in Ceylon and worked to restore its holy places in India.

He grew up in a Christian-run colonial school system and was drawn to the Theosophists Henry Steel Olcott and Helena Blavatsky, who were promoting Buddhism in Ceylon. He took the name Anagarika, "homeless one", a new role between monk and layman.

In 1891 he visited Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha gained enlightenment, and found it neglected and under the control of a Hindu abbot. He founded the Maha Bodhi Society to win it back for Buddhists, a long legal struggle. In 1893 he spoke at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago, alongside Vivekananda, and he later spread Buddhism in Britain and the United States.

At home he preached a proud, reformed Buddhism tied to Sinhala identity. It helped awaken anti-colonial feeling, but it also fed the Sinhala Buddhist nationalism behind later laws such as the Sinhala Only Act.
